items.name: Minoan & Mycenaean
items.description: The Minoan civilisation on Crete (c. 3000–1450 BCE) was Bronze Age Europe's first advanced culture, known for its palace complexes at Knossos, linear script, and vibrant frescoes. The Mycenaeans on mainland Greece absorbed and supplanted them; their civilisation of warrior kings, palace economies, and epic warfare is preserved in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey. The Bronze Age collapse (c. 1200 BCE) destroyed Mycenaean civilisation, leading to a 'Dark Age' from which Classical Greece emerged.

items.name: Archaic & Classical Greece
items.description: The Archaic period saw the rise of the polis (city-state), colonisation of the Mediterranean, and the Olympic Games (776 BCE). Classical Athens produced democracy, philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle), drama (Sophocles, Euripides), history (Herodotus, Thucydides), and the Parthenon. The Persian Wars (490, 480 BCE) forged Greek identity; the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) between Athens and Sparta exhausted both. Philip II of Macedon unified Greece before his assassination.

items.name: Hellenistic & Roman Greece
items.description: Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE) spread Greek culture from Egypt to India, creating the Hellenistic world where Greek became the common language of scholarship. After his death, his generals divided the empire. Rome gradually absorbed Greek territories, but 'captive Greece took captive its rude conqueror' — Roman culture was profoundly Hellenised. Athens became the philosophical capital of the Roman world; Corinth a major commercial centre.

items.name: Byzantine Era
items.description: With Constantine's transfer of the Roman capital to Constantinople (330 CE), Greece became the core of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire. Greek became the official language; Orthodox Christianity the state religion. Thessaloniki was the empire's second city. Byzantium preserved classical learning through the medieval period. The empire gradually shrank under pressure from Slavic migrations, Arab invasions, and Crusader attacks until the final Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453.

items.name: Slavs, Avars and the Byzantine themes
items.description: From the 580s Avar and Slavic raids broke the late Roman order in Greece. Slavic groups settled much of the interior and the western Peloponnese, while the Byzantines held the walled coastal towns: Thessalonica survived sieges recorded in the Miracles of Saint Demetrius (c. 586, 615–618, 676–678), and Monemvasia was founded on its rock as a refuge. The empire organised what it held into military provinces, the themes: Hellas (by the 690s), the Peloponnese (c. 800), Cephalonia, Thessalonica and Nicopolis. Staurakios campaigned against the Slavs in 783, and the failed Slavic siege of Patras (805 or 807) was followed by resettlement and conversion; by the 10th century the Slavs of Greece were largely Hellenised, apart from mountain groups such as the Melingoi and Ezeritai of the Taygetus.

periods.name: The themes of Hellas and the Peloponnese

items.name: Mount Athos, Samuel’s raids and Basil II
items.description: In the 10th century Greece shared in the Macedonian renaissance. Athanasius the Athonite founded the Great Lavra on Mount Athos in 963 with the support of Nikephoros II Phokas, and the Tragos typikon (972) organised the Holy Mountain; the monastery of Hosios Loukas in Phocis was built and decorated around 1011. Arab corsairs from Crete sacked Thessalonica in 904 until Nikephoros Phokas retook the island in 961. Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria raided Thessaly and the Peloponnese until Nikephoros Ouranos destroyed his army on the Spercheios in 997. After the Bulgarian war Basil II gave thanks in the Parthenon, then a church of the Virgin, in 1018.

periods.name: Arab raids and the reconquest of Crete

items.name: Normans, Venetians and the Komnenoi
items.description: Under the Komnenian emperors Greece was rich: Thebes and Corinth made silk, Thessalonica held the great Demetria fair, and the monastery of Daphni was decorated around 1100. It was also exposed. Robert Guiscard’s Normans landed at Corfu and Dyrrachium in 1081, and Alexios I bought Venice’s help with the chrysobull of 1082, which opened Byzantine ports to Venetian trade. Roger II of Sicily sacked Corinth and Thebes in 1147 and carried off their silk weavers, and William II’s Normans sacked Thessalonica in 1185. As central power weakened, local lords such as Leo Sgouros at Nauplia, Argos and Corinth ruled on their own by 1200.

items.name: The County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos
items.description: After the Norman admiral Margaritus of Brindisi took Cephalonia and Zakynthos (1185), the islands passed to Matthew Orsini, who acknowledged Venice and then the Prince of Achaea; his heirs, the Orsini counts palatine, ruled them for 150 years and took Epirus in 1318. In 1357 the Neapolitan Leonardo I Tocco received the county, and his family added Lefkada (1362), and under Carlo I Tocco Ioannina (1411) and Arta (1416), styling themselves despots of Epirus. Ioannina fell to the Ottomans in 1430 and Arta in 1449. Leonardo III Tocco fled to Italy when the Ottomans took the islands in 1479; Venice took Zakynthos in 1485 and Cephalonia in 1500.

sources.title: Wikipedia — County palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos

periods.name: Despots of Epirus and the fall

items.name: The Fourth Crusade and the Frankish conquest
items.description: The Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in April 1204, and the crusaders and Venice divided the empire on paper in the Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae. Boniface of Montferrat made Thessalonica his kingdom and marched south in 1204–1205, taking Thessaly, Boeotia and Attica; his vassal Othon de la Roche became lord of Athens. William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin conquered the Peloponnese and beat its Greek and Slavic defenders at the Olive Grove of Kountouras (1205). Leo Sgouros held out on Acrocorinth until his death in 1208. Venice took the ports it wanted (Modon and Coron, 1207), bought Crete and let its nobles seize the islands. This age of Latin rule is called the Frankokratia.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Boniface I, Marquis of Montferrat
Wikipedia — Battle of the Olive Grove of Kountouras

periods.name: Fall of Constantinople and the partition

items.name: The Kingdom of Thessalonica
items.description: Boniface of Montferrat, leader of the Fourth Crusade, took Thessalonica in 1204 and ruled a kingdom reaching from Macedonia over Thessaly, with the new lords of Athens, Euboea and the Peloponnese as his vassals. He was killed fighting the Bulgarians in 1207, leaving an infant son, Demetrius; a revolt of the Lombard barons was put down by the Latin emperor Henry in 1209. Michael I of Epirus took Larissa and much of Thessaly around 1212, and his brother Theodore Komnenos Doukas took the rest piece by piece, Serres in 1221, until Thessalonica surrendered in December 1224. A crusade to recover it in 1225 failed.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Boniface I, Marquis of Montferrat

items.name: The Principality of Achaea
items.description: William of Champlitte and Geoffrey I of Villehardouin conquered the Peloponnese (the Morea) in 1205, and the Villehardouin princes ruled it from Andravida with the port of Glarentza and castles at Chlemoutsi, Karytaina and Kalamata; its feudal court and laws are described in the Chronicle of the Morea and the Assizes of Romania. William II of Villehardouin built Mystras in 1249, but after his capture at Pelagonia (1259) he ceded Mystras, Monemvasia and the Mani to the Byzantines (1262), who pushed into Arcadia. Under the Angevins of Naples, the Navarrese Company (from 1381) and the last Zaccaria princes the principality shrank, until Constantine Palaiologos took Glarentza (1428), Patras (1430) and the remnant (1432).

items.name: The Duchy of Athens
items.description: Othon de la Roche, a Burgundian knight, was given Athens and Thebes by Boniface of Montferrat in 1205; his family ruled Attica and Boeotia from Thebes, with Argos and Nauplia as a fief of Achaea from 1212, and took the title of duke. In 1311 the Catalan Company, mercenaries cheated of their pay, destroyed the Frankish knighthood at Halmyros and took the duchy; they added the Duchy of Neopatras in Thessaly (1319) and put Athens under the Crown of Aragon. The Florentine Nerio Acciaioli took the Acropolis in 1388. The Acciaioli held on as Ottoman vassals until Omar Turakhan took Athens in 1456; the Acropolis surrendered in 1458, and Mehmed II visited the city.

items.name: The Despotate of Epirus
items.description: Michael Komnenos Doukas, a cousin of the deposed emperors, made Arta the capital of a Greek state in Epirus and Aetolia after 1204, took Corfu in 1214 and Larissa about 1212. His brother Theodore took Thessalonica in 1224 and was crowned emperor there, but his defeat by Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria at Klokotnitsa in 1230 ended the Empire of Thessalonica. Michael II restored the despotate at Arta, lost the Battle of Pelagonia to Nicaea in 1259, and saw Thessaly split off under his son John Doukas (1268). The Italian Orsini of Cephalonia took Epirus in 1318; the Byzantines annexed it in 1337 and Stefan Dušan’s Serbs in 1348. Later rulers were Serbs at Ioannina, Albanian lords at Arta and finally the Tocco, who held Ioannina (1411–1430) and Arta (to 1449) before the Ottomans took all.

items.name: The Duchy of the Archipelago
items.description: Marco Sanudo, a Venetian nephew of Doge Enrico Dandolo, seized Naxos and the central Cyclades in about 1207 and ruled them as Duke of the Archipelago, under the Latin emperor rather than Venice; other Venetian families took Andros, Tinos, Santorini and the smaller islands as fiefs. The Sanudo were followed by the Crispi in 1383. Corsairs, Catalan and Turkish raids and the Black Death emptied many islands. Hayreddin Barbarossa made the duke an Ottoman tributary in 1537; in 1566 Selim II gave the duchy to his Jewish favourite Joseph Nasi, and it was annexed outright when Nasi died in 1579.

items.name: Venetian Crete: the Kingdom of Candia
items.description: Venice bought Crete from Boniface of Montferrat in 1204, drove out the Genoese adventurer Enrico Pescatore and settled colonists from 1211, ruling from Candia (Heraklion) as the Regno di Candia. Cretan revolts were frequent, and in 1363 even the Venetian settlers rose with the Greeks in the Revolt of Saint Titus. Over time the two communities mixed, and after 1453 Crete became a refuge for Greek scholars; the Cretan Renaissance produced icon painters such as Michael Damaskinos and Domenikos Theotokopoulos (El Greco), and Vitsentzos Kornaros’s Erotokritos. Venice built the great walls of Candia. The Ottomans landed in 1645, took Chania and Rethymno, and Candia fell in 1669 after a siege of more than twenty years.

items.name: Byzantine Mystras and the Despotate of the Morea
items.description: In 1262 the captive prince William II of Villehardouin handed Mystras, Monemvasia and the Mani to Michael VIII Palaiologos, and from these the Byzantines slowly retook the Peloponnese. In 1349 John VI Kantakouzenos made his son Manuel the first despot of the Morea, and the despotate became the most vital part of the late empire: Mystras grew into a city of churches and palaces where the philosopher Gemistos Plethon taught. The despots rebuilt the Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus (1415) and conquered the last Frankish lands (1428–1432). Constantine Palaiologos ruled here before becoming the last emperor in 1449. After Murad II broke the Hexamilion (1446), the despotate paid tribute; the brothers Thomas and Demetrios quarrelled, and Mehmed II annexed it in 1460.

items.name: The Knights of Rhodes
items.description: The Knights Hospitaller, a crusading order that had lost the Holy Land, conquered Rhodes from the Byzantines between 1306 and 1310 and made it their headquarters, adding Kos, Leros, Kalymnos and the other islands of the Dodecanese and the castle of Bodrum on the mainland. Under their grand masters Rhodes became a fortress city, with the Palace of the Grand Master and the Street of the Knights. The knights beat off the Mamluks (1444) and Mehmed II’s great siege of 1480. In 1522 Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Rhodes for six months, and the knights surrendered on terms and left for Malta.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes

items.name: Civil wars, Zealots and Serbs
items.description: From 1321 the empire tore itself apart in civil wars, and its neighbours advanced into Greece. In Thessalonica the Zealots, an anti-aristocratic party, ran the city as a near-republic from 1342 to 1350. Andronikos III annexed Thessaly (1333) and Epirus (1337), but Stefan Dušan of Serbia took Macedonia, Epirus and Thessaly by 1348 and was crowned emperor; his half-brother Simeon Uroš ruled Epirus and Thessaly from Trikala. In those years monks led by Athanasios built the monasteries of Meteora on their rock pillars. The Ottomans, first brought into Europe as allies in the civil wars, crushed the Serbian lords at the Maritsa in 1371, took Serres (1383) and Thessalonica (1387), and overran Thessaly in 1393.

items.name: The Venetian Ionian Islands
items.description: Venice ruled Kythira (Cerigo) from 1363 and Corfu from 1386, took Zakynthos in 1485 and Cephalonia and Ithaca in 1500, and Lefkada in 1684. The islands were never Ottoman after 1500, apart from Kythira in 1715–1718: Corfu beat off great Ottoman sieges in 1537 and 1716, defended in 1716 by Johann Matthias von der Schulenburg. Venetian rule left an Italian-speaking nobility, the Libro d’Oro, olive and currant plantations, and a Greek culture open to Italy; Ugo Foscolo and Dionysios Solomos were born on Zakynthos. The French ended Venetian rule in 1797.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Venetian rule in the Ionian Islands

items.name: The Ottoman conquest of Greece
items.description: After the Ottomans took Thessalonica (1387, and finally in 1430 from the Venetians, who had held it since 1423) and Thessaly (1393), the rest of Greece fell over seventy years. Murad II broke the Hexamilion wall in 1446; Athens fell in 1456 and the Acropolis in 1458; Mehmed II conquered the Despotate of the Morea in 1460 and took Mytilene (1462). In the Ottoman–Venetian war of 1463–1479 he took Negroponte (1470) and the Tocco islands (1479), and in the war of 1499–1503 the Ottomans took Lepanto (1499) and Venice’s Messenian forts of Modon, Coron and Navarino (1500). Christian Greeks became tax-paying subjects; boys were taken in the devshirme, and the conquest left the Orthodox Church as the community’s leader.

items.name: Ottoman Greece
items.description: Most of Greece came under Ottoman rule between 1453 and 1460. The Orthodox Church preserved Greek identity under Ottoman rule. The Phanariot Greeks (wealthy Constantinople merchants) served as Ottoman administrators and translators. Greek merchants and intellectuals across the diaspora kept Hellenic culture alive. The Enlightenment and French Revolution inspired Greek nationalists; secret societies like the Filiki Eteria planned revolution.

items.name: Klephts, armatoloi and the Orthodox millet
items.description: Under Ottoman rule Orthodox Christians formed the Rum millet, led by the Patriarch of Constantinople, and villages ran much of their own affairs through notables (kodjabashis). Christian militias, the armatoloi, policed the mountain passes for the Ottomans, while outlaws in the mountains, the klephts, raided and were celebrated in folk songs; the two groups often swapped places, and both provided the captains of 1821. Mountain and island communities such as the Mani, Souli, Sphakia, Hydra and Spetses kept wide self-rule. The church schools and the monasteries kept Greek letters alive.

items.name: Venice against the Ottomans: Preveza and Lepanto
items.description: In the war of 1537–1540 Suleiman’s admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa besieged Corfu (1537), took the Venetian islands of the Aegean, and beat the Holy League’s fleet at Preveza (1538); Venice gave up Nauplia and Monemvasia, its last Peloponnesian towns, in 1540. Selim II’s attack on Venetian Cyprus in 1570 brought a new Holy League of Spain, Venice and the Pope, and on 7 October 1571 its galleys under John of Austria destroyed the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras off Lepanto (Nafpaktos), the last great galley battle. Venice still made peace in 1573 and gave up Cyprus.

items.name: The Cretan War and the siege of Candia
items.description: In 1645 an Ottoman fleet landed on Venetian Crete and took Chania; Rethymno fell in 1646, and in 1648 the Ottomans began the siege of Candia. Venice held the city by sea for over twenty years, blockading the Dardanelles and winning naval battles, while French and other volunteers came to its aid. In 1667 Grand Vizier Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed Pasha came to press the siege himself, and Francesco Morosini surrendered Candia in September 1669. Venice kept only the island forts of Grambousa, Souda and Spinalonga, lost in 1715.

items.name: Phanariots, merchants and the Greek Enlightenment
items.description: From the late 17th century Greek families of the Phanar quarter of Constantinople served the sultan as Grand Dragomans and, from 1711, as princes of Moldavia and Wallachia. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1774) let Ottoman Greek ships sail under the Russian flag, and merchant fleets from Hydra, Spetses and Psara grew rich in the Napoleonic wars; Greek merchant houses spread from Trieste and Vienna to Odessa. Their money paid for schools and books, and the Modern Greek Enlightenment of Eugenios Voulgaris, Nikiforos Theotokis and Adamantios Korais taught a new idea of the nation descended from the ancient Hellenes.

items.name: The Morean War and the Venetian Kingdom of the Morea
items.description: After the Ottoman defeat at Vienna (1683) Venice joined the Holy League, and Francesco Morosini took Lefkada (1684), then Coron (1685), Navarino, Modon, Argos and Nauplia (1686), and Patras, Corinth and Mystras (1687); Monemvasia fell in 1690. During the siege of Athens in September 1687 a Venetian mortar round blew up the Ottoman powder magazine in the Parthenon. The Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) left Venice the Kingdom of the Morea, run from Nauplia, which it resettled and surveyed. In 1715 the Ottomans retook the whole peninsula in a hundred-day campaign, confirmed at Passarowitz (1718).

items.name: The Orlov revolt
items.description: During the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774, Catherine the Great sent a fleet under Alexei Orlov to the Mediterranean to raise the Greeks. Orlov landed in the Mani in February 1770 and Greeks rose across the Peloponnese and Crete (Daskalogiannis in Sphakia), but the small Russian force failed before Modon and Tripolitsa and left; Albanian irregulars took terrible revenge on the Peloponnese for years. The Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman navy at Chesma (July 1770). The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1774) gave the Greeks an amnesty and Russia a claim to protect Orthodox subjects.

items.name: Ali Pasha, Souli and the Pashalik of Yanina
items.description: Ali Pasha of Tepelenë made Ioannina the capital of a near-independent pashalik from 1788, ruling Epirus, Thessaly and much of mainland Greece and Albania. His court drew Greek scholars and foreign visitors, Byron among them (1809). The Souliotes, an Orthodox Albanian clan in the mountains of Thesprotia, resisted him for years until Souli fell in December 1803; women of Souli are said to have danced off the cliff of Zalongo rather than be taken. Ali seized Preveza and Parga from the coast and courted Napoleon and Britain. The sultan’s war against him from 1820 helped the Greek revolution start; Ali was killed at Ioannina in January 1822.

items.name: Rigas Feraios and the revolutionary idea
items.description: Rigas Velestinlis, called Feraios, a Thessalian secretary in the Phanariot courts of Bucharest, wrote in Vienna a revolutionary programme for a republic of all the Balkan peoples on the French model: his Thourios war hymn, his Charta of Greece and a constitution, printed in 1797. Betrayed while carrying them to Greece, he was handed over by the Austrians and strangled with his companions in the Nebojša Tower at Belgrade in June 1798, becoming the first martyr of Greek independence.

items.name: French and Russian Ionian Islands: the Septinsular Republic
items.description: When Napoleon ended the Republic of Venice in 1797, the Treaty of Campo Formio gave the Ionian Islands to France. A Russian and Ottoman fleet under Fyodor Ushakov took them in 1798–1799 after the siege of Corfu, and in 1800 the Treaty of Constantinople made them the Septinsular Republic, the first autonomous Greek state of modern times, under Ottoman suzerainty and Russian protection; the young Ioannis Kapodistrias was one of its secretaries of state. At Tilsit (1807) Russia returned the islands to France; the British took Zakynthos, Cephalonia and Kythira in 1809 and Lefkada in 1810, and the French held Corfu until 1814. In 1815 the islands became the United States of the Ionian Islands under British protection.

sources.title: Wikipedia — French rule in the Ionian Islands (1797–1799)
Wikipedia — United States of the Ionian Islands

items.name: The Filiki Eteria
items.description: The Filiki Eteria (Society of Friends) was founded in Odessa in 1814 by three Greek merchants, Nikolaos Skoufas, Emmanouil Xanthos and Athanasios Tsakalof, as a secret society to free Greece. It spread among merchants, Phanariots, klephts and island shipowners, hinting that Russia was behind it. Its leader from 1820, Alexander Ypsilantis, a general in the Russian army, crossed the Pruth into Moldavia on 6 March 1821 to start the revolution; his army was beaten at Drăgășani in June, but by then the Peloponnese had risen.

items.name: The rising of 1821
items.description: In March 1821 the Peloponnese rose: Petros Mavromichalis and Theodoros Kolokotronis took Kalamata on 23 March, Patras and Kalavryta rose, and the revolution spread to Roumeli, Hydra, Spetses and Psara. Kolokotronis’s Greeks took Tripolitsa, the Ottoman capital of the Morea, in September 1821 and killed most of its Muslim and Jewish people. The First National Assembly at Epidaurus declared independence in January 1822. The Ottomans answered with the massacre of Chios (April 1822); Kanaris burned the Ottoman flagship in revenge, and Kolokotronis destroyed Dramali Pasha’s army at the Dervenakia passes in July 1822.

sources.title: Wikipedia — First National Assembly at Epidaurus

items.name: Greek War of Independence
items.description: The Greek Revolution (1821) began on 25 March — now Greece's national day. The war attracted Philhellenes from across Europe, including Lord Byron, who died at Missolonghi. Ottoman reprisals were brutal, including the massacres of Chios (1822) and Missolonghi (1826). European powers — Britain, France, and Russia — intervened at the Battle of Navarino (1827), destroying the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet. Greek independence was recognised in 1830; a Bavarian prince became King Otto.

items.name: Ibrahim, Missolonghi and Navarino
items.description: After two years of civil war among the Greeks, the sultan called in Muhammad Ali of Egypt. His son Ibrahim Pasha landed at Modon in February 1825 with a modern army and swept over the Peloponnese. Lord Byron had died of fever at Missolonghi in April 1824; the town held out for a year against Reşid Mehmed Pasha and Ibrahim until its people tried to break out on the night of 22 April 1826, and most were killed. Athens fell in 1827. Moved by philhellenes, Britain, France and Russia sent a fleet to force an armistice, and on 20 October 1827 it destroyed the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet in the bay of Navarino.

items.name: Kapodistrias and the new state
items.description: Ioannis Kapodistrias, the Corfiot former foreign minister of Russia, landed at Nauplia in January 1828 as the first governor of Greece, with Aegina and then Nauplia as capitals. A French expedition cleared Ibrahim’s army from the Morea (1828), and the London Protocol of February 1830 declared Greece an independent state. Kapodistrias founded schools, a national bank and a currency, the phoenix, but his centralising rule angered the island shipowners and the Mani clans, and he was assassinated by two Mavromichalis kinsmen at Nauplia in October 1831. The Treaty of Constantinople (1832) set the border on the line from Arta to Volos, and the Bavarian prince Otto arrived as king in February 1833.

items.name: Modern Greece
items.description: Modern Greece expanded gradually — acquiring Thessaly (1881), Macedonia and Crete (1912–13), and Thrace after WWI. The Asia Minor Catastrophe (1922) ended Greek presence in Anatolia after 3,000 years. WWII brought brutal Axis occupation and devastating civil war (1946–1949). Military junta ruled 1967–1974. Greece joined the EU (1981) and eurozone (2001). The 2010 debt crisis led to severe austerity. Greece's ancient legacy continues to shape Western civilisation.
